arguments.text:
As the Scientific Opponent, I will present my case in support of the claim that no drugs target the same proteins in our cells that the novel coronavirus does. The novel coronavirus, SARS-CoV-2, interacts with various host proteins to facilitate its replication and survival. Research has shown that identifying potential therapeutic targets is crucial for developing effective treatments against COVID-19 (Evidence 15, Source: 38370514). A study published in Frontiers in Genetics used a structural-based similarity approach to identify potential therapeutic targets for COVID-19 by analyzing the similarity between SARS-CoV-2 and human host proteins (Evidence 33, Source: 38370514).

The evidence suggests that the proteins targeted by SARS-CoV-2 are unique and not typically targeted by existing drugs. For instance, a study published in BMC Molecular and Cell Biology identified a druggable binding pocket in the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2, which could be a potential target for existing drugs (Evidence 1, Source: 32611313). However, this does not necessarily mean that existing drugs are currently targeting these proteins. In fact, research has highlighted the need for further investigation into the development of therapeutics that target SARS-CoV-2 proteins (Evidence 29, Source: 34198320).

Furthermore, various studies have emphasized the importance of understanding the interactions between SARS-CoV-2 proteins and host proteins to identify potential therapeutic targets (Evidence 2, Source: 34294141; Evidence 31, Source: 33605735). The lack of existing drugs that target the same proteins as SARS-CoV-2 highlights the need for continued research into the development of effective treatments against COVID-19. Therefore, based on the available evidence, it is reasonable to conclude that no drugs currently target the same proteins in our cells that the novel coronavirus does.

In opposition to the claim that no drugs target the same proteins in our cells that the novel coronavirus does, it is essential to highlight the growing body of evidence indicating that existing pharmaceuticals can indeed interact with and affect the proteins utilized by SARS-CoV-2 for its replication and infectivity. For instance, a study published in *BMC Molecular and Cell Biology* (Evidence 1, Source: 32611313) identified a druggable binding pocket within the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2, suggesting that certain existing drugs could potentially interfere with the viral infectivity processes. This finding illustrates that there are indeed pharmacological agents capable of targeting viral proteins, which may, in turn, influence the host cell proteins involved in the viral life cycle.

Moreover, the genome-wide analysis of protein-protein interactions conducted in a study published in *Cell & Bioscience* (Evidence 2, Source: 34294141) underscores the potential for existing drugs to be repurposed for targeting the interactions between SARS-CoV-2 proteins and host proteins. This research provides a foundational understanding that not only supports the identification of potential therapeutic targets but also suggests that some existing drugs may already have the capability to target these interactions. The assertion that no drugs currently target the same proteins as SARS-CoV-2 is therefore unfounded, as evidence to the contrary indicates that there are pathways and mechanisms through which existing therapeutics can be effective against the virus by targeting shared protein interactions. This highlights the urgent need for continued research into drug repurposing and the development of novel therapeutics aimed at mitigating COVID-19.
